trap.title: Technique: Escaping the Trap of Unrealistic Expectations
trap.description: This article explores the guilt that arises from setting unrealistic demands on yourself and constant self-criticism. It describes methods for reframing internal attitudes and replacing “should” statements with a more helpful understanding of your actual capabilities and desires. You’ll find practical advice on letting go of self-blame and building a more compassionate relationship with yourself and your mistakes.

texts: Guilt often stems from the unrealistic demands you place on yourself, manifesting in thoughts such as:
• “I should do this.”
• “I should act this way.”
• “I should be like this.”
• “I shouldn’t have done that.”
• “I should have seen this coming.”
Unrealistic demands involving “should” statements can lead to guilt and unrealistic expectations.
These demands imply that you must be perfect or all-knowing, which is simply unrealistic.
They might include the idea that you should always be happy or satisfied, which only serves to intensify feelings of failure.

<important>There are also demands based on the assumption that you know everything and can predict the future. This creates false expectations and guilt rather than helping you solve problems.</important>
The essence of this technique is to realize that blaming yourself is counterproductive and that these unrealistic demands are inherently unfair.
They only create feelings of guilt and helplessness instead of helping you solve a problem or achieve success.
To avoid constant self-blame, try letting go of these demands and being more realistic about your expectations for yourself and your life.
Of course, shifting your mindset doesn’t happen overnight—it might not even happen in a month. But consistent work on yourself leads to real change.
<q author="Bertrand Russell">Any sense of guilt implies self-judgment, and this is fundamentally wrong. A person should recognize their mistakes without falling into self-flagellation.</q>
So, what can you do right now to ease the guilt caused by these high expectations?

• A simple but effective way to escape unrealistic self-demands is to replace “should” with phrases like “It would be nice if...” or “If I could, I would...” These are often more realistic and less distressing.

For example, instead of saying “I should make my wife happy,” you could say: “It would be great if I could make my wife happy since she’s upset. I can ask her what’s wrong and think about how I might be able to help.”
Or instead of “I shouldn’t have eaten that ice cream,” you can say: “It would have been better if I hadn’t eaten that ice cream, but it’s not the end of the world.”
• Avoid ruminating on the past. Instead of thinking, “I should have...” or “If only I could...”, try thinking: “Next time, I will do it differently.”
People struggling with guilt often find themselves ruminating on what might have been, but you should try to avoid this.
If you catch yourself doing this, stop immediately and rephrase it to “Next time, I will...”
That’s it. No more “should haves.”

• The Reality Method helps you check if your demands align with reality. When you tell yourself “I shouldn’t have done that,” you are likely thinking that you truly shouldn’t have done it, and saying this to yourself might make you feel better.
However, in reality, the opposite is true: you did exactly what you had to do, but admitting this to yourself will only make you feel disappointed.
For example, you’ve started a diet to lose weight, you eat something extra, and now you blame yourself: “I shouldn’t have eaten that chocolate bar.”
But in reality, you had a craving. Perhaps you were stressed and instinctively wanted comfort food to boost your mood, making it very difficult to resist.
People often use food to cope with negative emotions. When you are trying to break a habit or lose weight, the main thing standing in your way is the belief that you are losing control.

<important>The feeling of losing control is directly linked to your “shoulds” and “shouldn’ts.” If you crave something unhealthy, you tell yourself you “shouldn’t” even want it, and that you “should” give up all unhealthy food once and for all without ever slipping up.</important>
And then, to feel better, you end up eating that chocolate bar. This approach to weight loss is unlikely to work; it will only leave you feeling guilty and overwhelmed.
Once you learn to stop forbidding yourself things, you will be able to let them go without feeling like you’re fighting against yourself.

• People prone to excessive guilt can be easily manipulated by others to achieve their own goals. Think about it: how many times have you agreed to something you didn’t really want to do just to please someone or to avoid hurting their feelings? It’s important to set personal boundaries and learn how to say “no.”
Example: A young woman lives with her parents and brother and earns a good salary. Her brother works part-time jobs from time to time.
He has an addiction to material things: he’s constantly buying new things, even though he doesn’t have enough money to cover it.
His sister realizes this isn’t the best way to manage money, but she keeps lending him money because she believes siblings should help each other—it’s just how their family is.

The woman is afraid to refuse her brother because she fears it might ruin their relationship. She practiced a difficult conversation with a friend beforehand and realized that saying “no” wasn’t as scary as it seemed.
Before you set your boundaries—whether by refusing a demand or standing your ground to avoid a social visit you don’t want—you can role-play the difficult conversation or write it out in your notes.
This allows you to predict a likely communication scenario and figure out the best way to decline, which might also help you realize that saying “no” isn’t actually that frightening.
It will take time for the right neural pathways to form in your brain so that you have the courage and skill to say “no” diplomatically yet firmly, and to practice this skill when the moment comes.
• Distinguishing Responsibility
Sometimes we take responsibility for the misfortunes and failures of others.
In these situations, it is important to figure out who is actually responsible for what happened. For example, are you truly to blame if your child gets poor grades?
This is where confusion often arises between your influence on a child and your control over them.
To learn how to distinguish responsibility, you can use the three-column method, which is a shortened version of an automatic thought journal.
In the first column, you write down distressing and judgmental thoughts; in the second, you note which cognitive distortions you notice; and in the third, you write down an adaptive response.
For example:
Column 1 (distressing and judgmental thoughts): “It’s my fault my child is getting bad grades. I won’t be able to help them succeed in school.”
Column 2 (cognitive distortions): personalization, overgeneralization.

Column 3 (adaptive response): “I am responsible for my role in raising my child, but I do not have full control over their academic success or failure. My child also has their own responsibility for their learning and studies. I can help, support, and motivate them, but the final result depends on their own work and effort.”

<important>It is important to understand that we cannot control every aspect of other people’s lives, even if they are under our influence. We are responsible for our own actions and the role we play in the lives of others, but we should not take full responsibility for their successes or failures.</important>

unemployment.title: Losing Your Job—and Slipping into Depression?
unemployment.description: This article explores the psychological and social impact of sudden job loss, tracing the emotional roller coaster that often follows. Through the story of Alexander, who spent years working at a successful company, it examines the struggle with depression, diminished self-esteem, and career setbacks. It also offers ways to move through these challenges, emphasizing the importance of support and self-respect during difficult times.

texts: Sudden job loss is a major stressor for most people. When a layoff or redundancy is announced, many feel as though their life has “collapsed.” This is understandable, as your life changes fundamentally in several ways:
• your financial situation
• your social status
• your daily routine
• your short-term and long-term plans
Work provides certain obligations, structure, and social interaction—it is, in short, something that supports us.

Unemployment, however, can feel like a freefall without a safety net. You are left alone with yourself, facing empty days, bills you may soon struggle to pay, and the endless wait for interview invitations—feeling a flicker of hope before a meeting, only to face another rejection. It is a disheartening picture.
Losing a job is experienced much like any other loss, and those who face it often go through the stages of grief.
<q author="Bob Marley">When one door closes, don’t you know that many others open.</q>
First comes shock, deep confusion, and not knowing what to do. Then comes anger—at yourself and at those who let you go.

There may also be bargaining: “What if I can fix this? What if they take me back?” And finally, depression. While these feelings are certainly “real,” that doesn’t mean they justify falling into a depressive state.
The reason for such an emotional reaction lies in the belief that personal worth and the ability to be happy are directly tied to professional success.
Within this value system, it seems logical to assume that emotional distress is inevitably linked to financial loss, career setbacks, or bankruptcy.
If you feel this way, Alexander’s story might resonate with you. Alexander is a 47-year-old father of three who worked for 17 years at the same successful company as his father-in-law.

A couple of years before his depression set in, disagreements arose between him and his father-in-law regarding the management of the company. In a fit of anger, Alexander resigned, thereby giving up his share in the business.
Over the next two years, he moved from one job to another, but he couldn’t find anything that felt worthwhile, either financially or emotionally.

<important>It felt as though nothing was working out, and he began to see himself as a failure. His wife had to take on full-time work to make ends meet, which only intensified Alexander’s sense of inadequacy, as he had always taken pride in being the family provider.</important>
As time passed, his financial situation worsened and his depression deepened as his self-esteem continued to plummet.
By the time Alexander decided to seek professional help, he had already been working for several months at a real estate company.

During this time, he had managed to lease a few buildings but hadn’t made a single sale. Since his salary depended on commissions, his income was low. During this period, Alexander struggled with depression and procrastination, spending entire days in bed, thinking:
“What’s the point? I’m a failure. Working is useless; I won’t succeed no matter what I do.”

During his third session with a psychologist, he shared that a wealthy friend wanted to buy property through him. The commission from such a sale would have boosted his career, increased his confidence, and significantly improved his finances.
Instead of seizing this opportunity, Alexander hesitated for several weeks. Why? Because he thought: "Selling commercial real estate is too difficult.
I've never done it before, and I definitely won't succeed. And if he changes his mind at the last minute, it will mean I'm not cut out for this business. It will mean that I am a complete failure."
Alexander’s management team thought highly of him and saw him as a capable salesperson, but he was unfairly harsh on himself.

Through subsequent sessions and working through his thoughts, Alexander agreed that he was overly self-critical. He realized this wasn’t helping him through this difficult period; instead, it was making things significantly worse.
He also realized he was using “double standards”: he was tolerant and supportive of others, but harsh and critical toward himself.
At first, he defended his perspective, as many demanding perfectionists do, arguing that being harder on himself than on others might somehow be beneficial.

<important>However, he quickly learned that his personal standards were actually unrealistic and destined for failure. If he had tried to sell a building and failed, he would have viewed it as a catastrophe. His tendency toward all-or-nothing thinking was a major problem.</important>
By the end of therapy, Alexander felt a sense of relief, realizing that his financial struggles over recent years did not automatically make him “a failure.”

This negative self-perception and sense of paralysis were the results of his extreme all-or-nothing thinking. His feeling of uselessness stemmed from focusing exclusively on the negative aspects of his life (a mental filter) and ignoring the many areas where he had succeeded (discounting the positive).

He realized he had been needlessly punishing himself for so long with the thought that he “should have done more,” and understood that financial difficulties did not diminish his human dignity. Ultimately, he recognized that his apathy and procrastination were merely symptoms of depression, not a reflection of his true self.
As he learned to provide adaptive responses to his negative thoughts, he was able to reduce the distortions in his harsh self-attitude, and his mood continued to improve.

He eventually left the real estate industry and opened a bookstore. He managed to cover his expenses, though despite significant personal effort, he couldn’t generate enough profit to sustain the business after the first trial year.

In this way, even though the external signs of success remained almost unchanged during this time, he was able to maintain his self-esteem and avoid depression. Despite his difficult financial situation, when he decided to “accept defeat” in his bookstore business, his self-respect remained intact.
Before his last session with a psychologist, Alexander wrote the following essay, which he decided to reread every morning before looking for a new job:
Why am I not useless?
• As long as I can do something for my own well-being and for others, I am not useless. As long as what I do can have a positive effect, I am not useless.

• As long as the fact that I am alive matters to even one person (and that person can be myself if needed), I am not useless. If giving love, understanding, friendship, support, sociability, advice, or comfort means anything at all, I am not useless.
• If I can respect my own opinions and intelligence, I am not useless.
• If others respect me, it is a pleasant bonus.
• If I have a sense of self-respect and dignity, I am not useless.
• If helping to provide a livelihood for my employees’ families means doing something good, I am not useless.
• If I do my best to help my clients and suppliers through my productivity and creativity, I am not useless.
• If my presence in this environment truly matters to others, I am not useless. I am not useless. I am inherently valuable!

If you are facing a similar problem or if Alexander’s automatic thoughts resonate with you, write a note to yourself about why you are not useless, why you are not a failure, and why you are valuable just as you are.

vitamins.title: False Depression: How Hormones and Vitamins Affect Our Emotional Health
vitamins.description: This article discusses how physical health, including hormonal balance and vitamin levels, can influence a person’s emotional state. It highlights that symptoms often associated with depression can be caused by physical issues, such as specific vitamin deficiencies or hormonal imbalances. The authors emphasize the importance of a comprehensive approach to diagnosing and treating mental health conditions, considering both psychological and physiological aspects.

texts: We aim to make this section as helpful as possible in improving and easing your emotional state. Therefore, it is important to discuss all possible causes of its changes.
When we talk about depression, we are referring to a specific set of symptoms mentioned earlier. However, these symptoms do not always indicate a mental health disorder.

It is important to remember that our body’s biological component plays a vital role not only in physical health but also in mental well-being. For instance, physical issues can significantly affect your emotional state, creating symptoms similar to depression.
Hormones are a prime example. They have a massive influence on a person’s behavior and psychological state.
Research in psychoendocrinology shows that the nervous and endocrine systems are interconnected, working together to maintain homeostasis (the body’s physiological balance).
<q author="Socrates">Take care of the body, so that the soul may wish to dwell within it.</q>
Because of this, any fluctuations in hormone levels can cause serious disruptions to your emotional well-being.
For example, an underactive thyroid can lead to depression, increased anxiety, and other mental health issues.
On the other hand, an overactive thyroid can cause mania, irritability, mood swings, and even psychosis.
Acromegaly, or excessive growth hormone production, can manifest as decreased mental activity and apathy combined with euphoria.
Thus, people with endocrine disorders face not only the physical challenges of their condition but also the risk of mental health disorders such as anxiety, depression, mania, confusion, and more.
In the mid-20th century, a whole scientific discipline emerged—psychoendocrinology—which studies the relationship between the human endocrine system and the psyche.

There is even a term, psychoendocrine syndrome, which refers to mental disturbances arising from endocrine diseases. These include mood disorders, asthenia, decreased mental activity, and changes in drives and instincts.
In addition to hormones, vitamins also have a significant impact on our well-being.
<important>Vitamin deficiency and depression might not seem directly related, but research shows the connection between them is much stronger than we might assume.</important>
You’ll likely agree that our bodies need vitamins to maintain metabolism. There are many of them, and each one is indispensable. When the body lacks something, a vitamin deficiency occurs.
Vitamin deficiency is a condition where the body lacks or completely lacks a certain vitamin.
Deficiencies in various vitamins can affect mental health in different ways, ranging from minor discomfort to frightening symptoms.

Research has shown that vitamin deficiency can contribute to the onset of anxiety and depression, and can also worsen symptoms in people with certain mental health conditions, such as obsessive-compulsive or bipolar disorder.
Even if you are healthy, a lack of certain vitamins can negatively affect your mood and emotional state.
Examples of vitamin deficiencies and their symptoms:
• Vitamin D: low mood, anxiety, fatigue, mood swings.
• Iron: weakness, fatigue, shortness of breath, dizziness, numbness.
• Vitamin B12: increased fatigue, anemia, insomnia, loss of appetite, digestive issues, muscle pain.
• Folic acid: fatigue, irritability, depression, weakness, apathy, lethargy, impaired cognitive function.
• B vitamins: increased fatigue, irritability, insomnia, mood swings, irregular heartbeat.
• Magnesium: weakness, headaches, anxiety, irregular heartbeat.
• Vitamin C: chronic fatigue, emotional instability.
And these are only some of the possible symptoms that can easily be mistaken for a depressive state.
Our personal stories confirm the importance of considering hormonal and vitamin balance when diagnosing mental health disorders.
One of our team members thought they were experiencing burnout, struggling with unexplained fatigue, worsening mood, and a lack of motivation.
But knowing that it could be related to hormones and vitamins, they consulted a doctor, identified a deficiency, completed a course of Vitamin D, and began to feel significantly better.
Another team member, a young woman experiencing symptoms similar to depression, was diagnosed with iron-deficiency anemia, the treatment of which led to a significant improvement in her condition.

She described her experience like this: "I constantly wanted to sleep, I didn't want to do anything, and I didn't want to talk to anyone. I suffered from terrible apathy, dizziness, and irritability. At one point, I really started to think I had depression, until I happened to get a routine blood test that revealed issues with my hemoglobin.

After that, I had additional tests that revealed an iron and ferritin deficiency. I had iron-deficiency anemia, but I thought it was depression. After a course of medication, I felt like myself again. My condition improved significantly."
By sharing these stories, we want to help you avoid misdiagnosis.
<important>So, if you feel low mood, fatigue, exhaustion, or any of the other symptoms mentioned above, pay attention not only to your mental health but also to your physical health.</important>
Consult a doctor, get a routine blood test, and check your vitamin and hormone levels. This might be all it takes to improve your emotional state.
